what_it_does: Large language models contain billions of numerical weights — the learned parameters that determine how the model thinks — and storing them in full precision (32-bit floating-point numbers) requires enormous amounts of memory. A common way to shrink models is to round each weight to a smaller, cruder number format (a process called quantization), but different groups of weights tolerate different amounts of rounding; forcing them all into the same format wastes accuracy. BitMoD solves this by choosing, for every small block of 128 weights, the specific number format from a menu of options (such as 4-bit integers or 4-bit floating-point variants) that introduces the least error for that particular block. On the hardware side, the chip processes weights one binary digit at a time rather than all at once — a technique called bit-serial arithmetic — so the same physical circuits can handle any of the number formats without needing separate dedicated hardware for each. A small on-chip unit then rescales the partial results back to full precision after each group is processed.
